transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Cornell University has named a former leader of the Justice Department to head an independent
investigation into how the New York School handles reports of sexual assault.
NPR's Jacqueline Diaz reports that includes the school's response to a woman who alleges
she was gang-raped at Cornell two years ago.
Former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates will lead the internal review into how
Cornell responded when the now former student reported being drugged and repeatedly raped
at a fraternity on campus.
Yates was picked by a newly formed special committee of the Cornell University Board
of Trustees.
She will also examine the school's policies on how it prevents in response to sexual harassment,
assault, and other misconduct on campus.
This all comes after a former student filed a lawsuit against the school last month.
The student, who goes by Jane Doe, alleges failings in how Cornell administrators handled
her case.
Yates's probe is separate from a reopening of the criminal case, which is being led by
New York AG Letitia James.
Jacqueline Diaz, NPR News.
Well, with the midterms less than a month away now, a new study warns of polls that
use artificial intelligence to answer for people.
St. Pierre's Windsor-Johnson reports the technology can confuse stereotypes with what
Americans actually think.
Researchers at the Pew Research Center gave an AI model profiles of real survey participants
and asked it to answer for them.
One striking miss involved soccer.
The model predicted 97 percent of Hispanic adults would follow the World Cup.
Among actual respondents, just 43 percent said they would.
Aaron Smith leads Pew's Data Labs team.
There were clearly instances where the model was leaning on stereotypes or beliefs that
might be common within a particular group, but are certainly not ubiquitous.
Smith says checking a poll's methodology, including whether researchers actually talk
to people and how they chose them, is crucial.
Windsor-Johnson, NPR News.
Saudi Arabia says two airports were hit in the latest conflict with Yemen's Houthi rebels,
fighters backed by an Iranian government that has been at war with the U.S. and Israel for
more than seven months.
And Pierre's Ayyaba Trawi says the Saudi Kingdom is enlisting allied support.
By nightfall, Saudi-backed forces in Yemen said that they had entered the Red Sea port
city of Mocha and pushed the Houthis out.
The Houthis, however, deny any loss of territory.
Now, this offensive comes around three weeks after the Houthis had swept into southwestern
Yemen, capturing Mocha and islands in Bab and Mandab.
That is the key Red Sea shipping route that Saudi Arabia had been using to export its
oil since the Strait of Hormuz to the east is blocked by Iran.
That's NPR's Ayyaba Trawi reporting.
From Washington, this is NPR News.
Student protesters clash with police in the French capital, as recorded by the Associated
Press, police fired tear gas into the crowds in multiple French cities today, as tens of
thousands of people rallied for more funding and other resources in schools.
A public comment period is wrapping up today on the Trump administration's controversial
plan to reverse a ban on logging in millions of acres of pristine national forests.
NPR's Kirk Sigler reports a so-called roadless rule dates back to the Clinton administration.
The Trump administration wants to overturn the roadless rule that bans new road building
on millions of acres of undeveloped national forest land, areas that had been set aside
for possible wilderness designations.
Travis Joseph with the Timber Group American Forest Resource Council says that rule is
outdated.
This is a 25-year-old administrative policy passed by an administration, not by Congress.
The Constitution gives Congress the power to make the laws and regulations that govern
public land.
Conservationists argue the rule is one of the only tools left to protect critical wildlife
and watersheds in Alaska and the West.
A final decision on its repeal is expected later this year.
Kirk Sigler, NPR News.
President Trump approved death by firing squad for former Army General Nidal Malik Hassan.
The ex-psychiatrist is on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth for the 2009 shootings
at Fort Hood, Texas.
Hassan killed 13 people in the shooting rampage and injured more than 30 other individuals.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.

topics.text: Cornell University names former acting Attorney General Sally Yates to lead investigation into sexual assault handling
Pew Research Center study warns AI polls confuse stereotypes with actual American opinions ahead of midterms
Saudi Arabia reports airports hit in latest conflict with Yemen's Houthi rebels backed by Iran
